title: Moments of mind
hook: consciousness as a stream of tiny moments, each arising and passing

segments.voice: Yesterday, four drawers: consciousness, mental factors, matter, and nibbana. Your line: four realities. Which drawer did the thing that bothered you end up in? Day one thousand sixty-seven.

A flip book is a small stack of paper with a drawing in the corner of every page. Each drawing is still. A stick figure with one leg forward. Then the same figure, the leg a little further. Then a little further. Hold the stack and riffle it with your thumb, and the figure runs. It looks like one smooth motion, but there's no running on any single page. The running happens in the flipping. Today the first drawer opens, and the Abhidhamma says the mind is a little like that flip book.
screen: `A DRAWING ON EVERY PAGE.` → `RIFFLE IT, AND IT RUNS.` → `NO RUNNING ON ANY ONE PAGE.`

segments.voice: Today's word is citta, usually put into English as mind, or consciousness: the knowing of something. First, the Abhidhamma's claim. Mind isn't one steady light left on all day. It's a stream of tiny moments of knowing, one at a time, each arising, staying for an instant, and passing away, followed by the next. The commentaries give each moment those three phases: arising, standing, dissolving. Second, the seed of this in the suttas. In the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha uses a picture. A monkey moving through a forest grabs a branch, lets it go, grabs another, lets that go. In paraphrase, he says what we call mind is like that: by day and by night, it arises as one thing and ceases as another. And in the Anguttara Nikaya, he says he can't point to anything that changes as quickly as the mind. Third, why it matters. If mind is one steady thing, then a bad mood can seem like a fact about who someone is. But if mind is moments, then the bad mood is a run of pages in the flip book, and the next page isn't drawn yet. The Dhammapada opens, in Max Müller's translation, with a line some readers hear alongside this: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts." Made up of moments, each one a chance. Fourth, the quiet surprise. Watched closely, the stream doesn't need a watcher behind it. The knowing of the itch is one moment. The knowing that you noticed it is the next. There's riffling, and figures running, and no one sitting inside the book.
screen: `ONE MOMENT OF KNOWING AT A TIME.` · `THE MONKEY IN THE FOREST.` · `THE NEXT PAGE ISN'T DRAWN YET.` · then, large: `NO ONE INSIDE THE BOOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: watch thoughts flicker. Sit, and let the breath settle. Don't chase thoughts and don't push them away. Just watch the screen of the mind the way you'd watch a road from a window. A thought appears. Notice it. Notice it go. A sound. Gone. A memory. Gone. A plan for dinner. Gone. If you get carried off on one, that's the monkey grabbing a branch; notice that too, and come back to watching. You're not trying to stop the flicker. Only to see that it flickers. The bell holds the time.
Citta. Consciousness, the knowing of something, which the Abhidhamma sees as a stream of tiny moments, each arising and passing. Today's word.
Your line: moment by moment. Today, when a mood seems permanent, remind yourself it's a run of pages, and the next page isn't drawn yet. Day one thousand sixty-seven.

howItsDone: In Theravada insight meditation, practitioners watch thoughts, sounds and sensations arise and pass, and teachers often explain what they see using the Abhidhamma's account of mind as a stream of moments.

fork.setup: a monkey is moving through the forest. it grabs a branch. what does it do next, in the Buddha's picture of the mind?
options: holds that branch and never lets go
lets it go and grabs another
climbs down and sits still forever
fork.reveal: it lets go and grabs another, and another: what we call mind, the Buddha says, arises as one thing and ceases as another, by day and by night.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit: mind, consciousness, the knowing of something.

trapdoor: what you thought: the mind is one thing, always on, like a lamp.
what it means: a stream of tiny moments of knowing, each arising and passing, like pages in a flip book.
what a scholar hears: the commentaries split each citta into arising, standing and dissolving (uppada, thiti, bhanga), building on the suttas' monkey simile.

sources.quoted: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 1.48 (nothing changes as quickly as the mind)
Abhidhammattha Sangaha IV (the three phases of a mind-moment)

notes: Dhammapada 1 quoted from Max Müller (SBE X, 1881). Confirm wording.
SN 12.61 monkey simile and AN 1.48 paraphrased; confirm references (AN numbering varies between editions).
Three phases of a mind-moment (uppada, thiti, bhanga) are commentarial; the script attributes them to 'the commentaries'. No figure for how many moments pass per second is given, on purpose.
'The stream doesn't need a watcher behind it' is the writer's plain rendering of anatta applied to citta. Confirm it is fair to the Theravada reading.
Editor: the Dhammapada 1 line is no longer said to 'lean on exactly this' (the verse is not about mind-moments); softened a line that told the listener what a mood feels like.
